summary: Specifies a simple file storage service run by UC Santa Barbara for other ARPANET users. After logging in, a user could allocate, update, replace, retrieve, space, delete and rename files with short primitive operations. It is a site-specific service description from 1971.

plainLanguage.summary: A tiny digital storage closet at Santa Barbara. You get a key, then you can put things in, take them out, throw them away, or give them new labels.

questions: what was the ucsb simple-minded file system
what file operations did ucsb offer over the network
how did users log in to smfs
subtitle: How a 1971 ARPANET site offered simple remote file storage through a small set of binary commands.

tldr.problem: Network users needed somewhere to keep files, and UC Santa Barbara wanted to offer a limited amount of secondary storage to the whole Network community.
tldr.mechanism: A user logs in by making a pair of connections to socket X'401' at site 3, then sends a stream of binary commands (allocate, update, replace, retrieve, space, delete, rename). Each command gets a response with a completion code.
tldr.outcome: It is a site-specific service description, not a general protocol. UCSB says it does not expect to become the file storage node of the Network.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 122 as Unknown, and it is updated by RFC 217, RFC 269, RFC 399 and RFC 431. The text describes a 1971 service at one site.

sections.title: The Simple-Minded File System
sections.content:
RFC 122 describes the Simple-Minded File System (SMFS), which UCSB offered to Network users. It sits at socket X'401', site 3, needs no accounting parameters, and talks through its NCP using the Host-Host protocol of August 3, 1970.

Files live on IBM 2316 disk packs of 29M 8-bit bytes each and are backed up to tape daily. The RFC is modest about it: UCSB does not expect to become the file storage node of the Network, only to make a limited amount of secondary storage available.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a small shared storage closet run by one university. It is not meant to hold everyone's stuff, just some of it.

sections.title: Logging In
sections.content:
A user opens a standard Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) connection to socket X'401', site 3. SMFS accepts the call, sends back a 32-bit receive socket number n, and closes that connection. It then opens two connections to the user, one from its send socket n+1 to the user's receive socket m, and one from its receive socket n to the user's send socket m+1. Once both exist, the user is logged in.

SMFS can serve up to ten users at once (an assembly-parameter maximum). It keeps the connections open indefinitely and closes them itself only on a bad op code or to signal end-of-data. Users should close the connections when finished.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on a well-known door, get told which two private doors to use, and then talk through those until you leave.

sections.title: Files and Primitive Operations
sections.content:
Files are sequential binary files from one bit up to 25 million bits. A filename is 1 to 36 characters from A to Z, 0 to 9 and blank, in EBCDIC or ASCII, upper or lower case, and case does not make names distinct. Each file can have an access password and a modification password, checked separately for retrieval and for changes.

The operations are ALF (allocate, which reserves name, space and passwords), UDF (append data), RPF (replace all contents), RTF (retrieve), SPF (skip a segment without sending its data), DLF (delete) and RNF (rename). FNO ends a series of retrievals so the next one starts at the first segment, and NOP is discarded. Only one user can modify a file at a time, while many may retrieve it together.

The RFC suggests rewriting a file safely by allocating a temporary file, filling it, deleting the original and renaming the new file.
sections.plainLanguage: You can reserve a shelf, add to it, empty and refill it, read it, skip ahead, throw it out or relabel it. A password can lock reading, writing, or both.

sections.title: Command and Response Streams
sections.content:
The input stream is a contiguous string of commands. Each starts with an 8-bit op code and a 16-bit flags field, followed by only the fields that command defines: filename, passwords, new filename, bit count and data. Filenames and passwords carry an 8-bit length first. SMFS keeps accumulators for filename, password and bit count, and flag bits let a command reuse the previous value instead of resending it.

Every command except FNO and NOP gets a response with an echoed op code and filename, a completion code and sometimes a bit count and data. Success returns a code equal to the op code. Failures use codes such as 32 (file not found), 35 (incorrect password) and 42 (end-of-data). An invalid op code is severe: SMFS sends X'FF' and the bad op code, then closes both connections.
sections.plainLanguage: You send short coded notes, and the closet answers each with a number. If the number matches your request code, it worked.
